column2: A permutation is a rearrangement that sends each item to exactly one position, with no collisions and no missing destinations. Imagine four numbered cards. We can describe a rearrangement by tracking where each label goes. Let's follow card one to its new position, then the card it displaced, until the trail closes.

Suppose one goes to three, three goes to four, and four goes back to one. We write the cycle one, three, four. The label two stays where it is, and we can omit that one-element cycle. The list is a loop, not a row of destinations: starting at three gives the same cycle, three, four, one. Reversing the direction usually gives a different permutation.

Now compute a composition. As before, the rightmost operation acts first. Take the cycle one, two, three after the swap one, two. Follow one: the swap sends it to two, then the three-cycle sends two to three. Follow three: it stays put under the swap, then moves to one. Follow two: it goes to one, then back to two. The composition swaps one and three and fixes two. Reversing the order gives a different swap.

To undo a cycle, run its arrows backwards. The inverse of one, three, four is one, four, three. If two cycles affect separate labels, they commute: each changes only positions the other leaves alone. Every trail in a finite permutation eventually returns to its starting label. It cannot first enter an earlier label in the middle, because that would give one destination two different inputs. So the trails form disjoint cycles. Their order and the starting point chosen within each loop do not change the permutation.

A transposition swaps just two labels. Every cycle can be built from transpositions. For example, the cycle one, three, four equals the swap one, four after the swap one, three, with the rightmost swap performed first. Check the path of each of the three labels. A cycle of length m can be built from m minus one transpositions, so every permutation can be built from swaps.
There may be many different swap descriptions of the same permutation. Can one description use an even number of swaps and another use an odd number? Predict before we prove it.

If the answer is no, parity belongs to the permutation itself, not to our chosen description. Here's one way to see why parity cannot change. Put distinct numbers x one through x n on the labels, and multiply all the differences x j minus x i for pairs with i less than j.

Swap the numbers on any two labels, and this product changes sign. The difference between the two swapped labels reverses. The two factors involving any other label exchange, sometimes both reversing signs, so their product stays the same. Factors that avoid both labels do not change at all. The magnitude stays the same.

After a sequence of swaps, that product has been multiplied by minus one once per swap. The final arrangement determines the final product, and the original product is not zero because the numbers are distinct. So two swap sequences reaching the same permutation must have the same parity. An even permutation requires an even number of swaps in every decomposition; an odd one requires an odd number in every decomposition.

Our square symmetries are permutations of its four corners, but not every permutation of four corners preserves a square. All twenty-four permutations form a group, and our eight square symmetries sit inside it as a subgroup. A quarter-turn is a four-cycle, so it is odd; a half-turn swaps two pairs of corners, so it is even. Now read the square's own moves as labels: r s is the swap two, four, and s r is the swap one, three. That is the same refusal to commute we saw on the tile.

In applications, a permutation might represent the positions of cards, the wires in a network, or the order in which data are rearranged. A composition predicts the combined effect, and the inverse tells us how to undo it. The group records what the moves do; it does not by itself guarantee that a physical device performs them without error. Next we'll ask when two groups with different-looking objects actually have the same structure.
